title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the blank verso of p.16 of a typescript. The neighbouring pages are Deligne's 'Courbes elliptiques : formulaire d'après J. Tate' (automorphisms of Weierstrass curves in characteristics 3 and 2 in §6; §7 'Anneau des formes modulaires entières', starting on p.17). The only content is a short handwritten blue-ink note. It reads: 'Cor : pour S plat sur Z, Γ(S,O_S)[...]', with a bracketed alternative '[ou seulement 2 et 3 non div. de 0]'.

In context, this sketches a corollary to Proposition 7.1. That proposition says the ring of integral modular forms (laws assigning to every genus-one curve over any base a section of ω^{⊗n}, compatibly with base change) is Z[c4,c6,Δ]/(c4^3 − c6^2 − 1728Δ).

The intended corollary is surely the following. Let S be flat over Z, or more weakly let 2 and 3 be non-zero-divisors on S. Then the ring of modular forms over S is Γ(S,O_S)[c4,c6,Δ]/(c4^3 − c6^2 − 1728Δ). The '[...]' is the polynomial ring with this relation, left unwritten.

Why it holds:
- A form over A = Γ(S,O_S) is determined by its value on the universal Weierstrass curve. That value is an isobaric polynomial over A in the a_i.
- After inverting 6 (or tensoring with Q), it is a polynomial in c4 and c6 (by 2.5).
- Because 2 and 3 are non-zero-divisors, nothing is lost on passing to A[1/6].
- The divisibility argument of the proof of 7.1 then applies with coefficients in A. That argument says: a polynomial in c4, c6, Δ vanishing identically mod 2 (resp. mod 3) is divisible by 2 (resp. 3).

The hypothesis is exactly what excludes characteristics 2 and 3. There the ring of forms is larger: it contains a1 (the Hasse invariant) in characteristic 2, and b2 in characteristic 3. The note records the natural base-change statement and its sharp hypothesis.
errors: No error. The statement is incomplete as written: the bracket '[...]' leaves the polynomial ring with the relation unspecified.

Strictly, the weaker hypothesis has to be applied with care. One needs the fact that a form over A is determined after inverting 6, i.e. that A injects into A[1/6]. That is precisely the condition that 2 and 3 are non-zero-divisors, so the condition is the right one.

ideas.what: Base change of the ring of integral modular forms (level 1) to a base on which 2 and 3 are non-zero-divisors: M_*(A) = A[c4,c6,Δ]/(c4^3 − c6^2 − 1728Δ).
ideas.modern_name: Ring of Katz/Deligne modular forms of level 1 over a general base; base change for M_*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Formulaire, LNM 476, 1975); Katz (p-adic properties of modular schemes and modular forms, 1973)
ideas.where_published: Deligne, 'Courbes elliptiques : formulaire d'après J. Tate', Modular Functions of One Variable IV, LNM 476 (1975), §7

deep.surprise_reason: A marginal note on a copy of Deligne's Formulaire. It records a routine base-change corollary of Prop. 7.1 with the obvious hypothesis (2 and 3 non-zero-divisors), and this is standard knowledge. Nothing new.
transcription_corrections: The 'S' is written as a script/curly letter (possibly 𝒮), followed by 'plat sur ℤ'.
The note is handwritten in blue ink on the verso of typescript p.16. '20' at bottom left is the archive page number, not part of the mathematics.
